newsitem.title: SPAIN: US explores use of Spain air base for transit.
newsitem.headline: US explores use of Spain air base for transit.

text.p: The United States has contacted Spain about using one of its air bases to provide logistical support and refuelling for transiting U.S. military aircraft, a U.S. embassy official in Madrid said on Saturday.

The Spanish daily El Mundo reported on Saturday that Washington and Madrid have been talking secretly about reinstalling U.S. Air Force (USAF) troops and planes to Torrejon and Zaragoza, two bases seen as strategically important staging grounds for conflicts in the Middle East and North Africa.
The U.S. embassy in Madrid and Spanish Defence Minister Eduardo Serra denied the report.
"We are not negotiating in secret with the Ministry of Defense to reinstall bases in Spain," said a senior U.S. embassy official in Madrid who asked not to be named.

"The U.S. Air Force has been in technical level contact with Spanish authorities to study the possibility that Zaragoza air base could be used for logistical and refuelling support for transiting U.S. military aircraft," the official added.
He said there was no talk about using Torrejon, a base the USAF dismantled in 1992, retiring the 72 fighter bombers F-16s deployed there.

"It's absolutely false," Defence Minister Eduardo Serra said of the El Mundo report in a radio interview on Saturday. He said there were no secret or open negotiations on reinstalling the U.S. Air Force.

Torrejon near Madrid and Zaragoza in the northeast were key staging grounds for U.S. attacks on Iraq during the 1991 Gulf War. The U.S. also launched its bombing raid on Libya in 1986 from Zaragoza, angering Spaniards.

The USAF pulled out all its planes stationed at the two bases in 1992, six years after the two countries signed a defence pact in 1988 to reduce the number of planes and cut the maximum number of U.S. troops in Spain to around 8,000 from 12,500.
The U.S. official said there was no discussion of rebasing any planes in Spain.

El Mundo said the U.S. considers Spanish bases to be better located strategically than others in Germany or Britain for operations in the Middle East and North Africa, the main arenas of world tension from where future threats to interests of the U.S. and its allies are likely to come.
"Just geographically, if you are flying out of the United States, Spain is an ideal landing place when moving on to much of Africa or the Middle East," the U.S. official said.
There are currently about 3,500 troops stationed in Spain, most of them naval forces at the Rota military base. There are no permanent planes based in Spain, U.S. diplomats said.
An air force base at Moron is the only one used now to support a fairly heavy traffic of transiting U.S. military flights, the embassy said.
